title: Data Manipulation Recognition Track — Junior
description: A 10-exercise junior recognition track. Read Pandas-style snippets, predict outputs, spot bugs that run without errors, and review a 30-line Bronze→Silver cleaning pipeline. Five modules: DM1 Filtering · DM2 Sorting · DM3 Reshaping · DM4 Casting · DM5 Cleaning. Foundations track — tool-agnostic where possible.

datasets.description: NordGrid meter readings (10–20 rows depending on exercise). Most exercises use a smaller inline sample shown in the Evidence panel; this file is the schema-level reference.
Substations reference (6 rows). Used in cleaning + type-casting exercises.

tasks.title: The Empty String Is Not A Null

description.context: Pandas treats two kinds of 'missing' very differently. A null is the special value NaN (or pd.NA) — Pandas marks the cell as 'no data here'. An empty string '' is a real string of length zero — Pandas treats it as a present value, just one with no characters. The method `notna()` only returns False for the null kind; it returns True for the empty string. The comparison `!= ''` only returns False for the empty string; for nulls, comparison-with-null returns null which Pandas treats as falsy in a boolean mask. So the two filters drop overlapping but DIFFERENT sets of rows. CSV readers commonly produce both kinds in the same column when upstream sources are inconsistent.
description.task: How many rows does each filter keep?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: A 10-row sample of NordGrid meter readings. Two rows have an empty string in `region`, two rows have a true null, and six rows have a regular region value.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Two candidate filters. Both are intended to 'keep only rows with a region'.
result_a = df[df['region'].notna()]
result_b = df[df['region'] != '']

fields.label: How many rows does each filter keep?
options: result_a keeps 8 rows, result_b keeps 8 rows — notna() and != '' are interchangeable ways to ask 'is there a value here', so both filters drop the same four rows (two empties + two nulls).

result_a keeps 8 rows, result_b keeps 6 rows — notna() drops only true nulls, so the two empty-string rows survive in result_a; != '' drops the empty strings (and the nulls compare as falsy), giving 6 rows in result_b.
result_a keeps 6 rows, result_b keeps 8 rows — != '' is the looser check because it only inspects the empty-string condition; notna() is the stricter filter and drops both nulls and empties.
result_a keeps 6 rows, result_b keeps 6 rows — Pandas treats '' and null as the same missing-value sentinel, so notna() and != '' end up dropping the same union of rows.
fields.correctAnswer: result_a keeps 8 rows, result_b keeps 6 rows — notna() drops only true nulls, so the two empty-string rows survive in result_a; != '' drops the empty strings (and the nulls compare as falsy), giving 6 rows in result_b.
fields.rationale: The two filters target different things. notna() returns True for any value that is not a true null — and the empty string '' is not a null, it is a real string of length zero. So the two empty-string rows (M-003, M-007) pass notna() and stay in result_a (8 rows). The != '' check returns False for those empty-string rows and null-when-compared-to-null for the nulls (also falsy), so result_b drops all four (6 rows). The most common Junior confusion is treating '' and null as the same kind of 'missing'; Pandas treats them as two distinct categories.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats notna() and != '' as the same operation. The exact misconception this exercise targets — '' is not a null in Pandas.

Option C: Reverses which filter is stricter. != '' is the stricter one because it drops both empties and nulls; notna() drops only nulls.

Option D: Conflates '' with null as a single 'missing' sentinel. Pandas keeps them distinct categories and the two methods disagree on which to treat as missing.

tasks.title: Three Filter Idioms, Three Different Behaviors

description.context: Pandas offers three common ways to subset a DataFrame and Junior engineers often assume they are interchangeable. Boolean mask indexing (`df[df['col'] > x]`) builds a True/False array and keeps the True rows. The `.query()` method takes a STRING expression that Pandas parses internally; it is row-filtering. The `.filter()` method has a misleading name — it does NOT filter rows by a predicate. It selects COLUMNS by name (or rows by INDEX label, but never by a value condition). Knowing what each idiom actually does matters because they can produce the same row count on a sample dataset for the wrong reason.
description.task: On the 10-row test dataset all three idioms produce 6 rows. Which statement about them is correct?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 10-row sample of NordGrid meter readings used by all three idioms below.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Three idioms, all targeting 'keep rows where daily_kw > 1000'.

# Idiom A — boolean mask indexing
result_a = df[df['daily_kw'] > 1000]

# Idiom B — the query() method with a string expression
result_b = df.query('daily_kw > 1000')

# Idiom C — the filter() method (often misused on rows; it actually filters columns)
result_c = df.filter(items=['daily_kw']).loc[df['daily_kw'] > 1000]

fields.label: On the 10-row test dataset all three idioms produce 6 rows. Which statement about them is correct?
options: All three idioms route through the same internal Pandas filter path and the choice between them is just style — boolean masking, query(), and filter() are documented as aliases for the same row-predicate operation.

Idiom B is the differentiator: query() fails on column names with spaces or hyphens because its string parser is restricted, while idioms A and C work on any column name and on this test dataset they all happen to produce 6 rows.

Idiom A returns a view, idiom B returns a copy, and idiom C returns a copy-of-a-subset — the row counts match by coincidence, but only A may trigger SettingWithCopyWarning, so A is the one to avoid in production.

Idiom C does not actually filter rows — DataFrame.filter() selects COLUMNS (here just daily_kw via items=[...]); the row predicate is done by the .loc[...] that follows. Same row count by coincidence, very different operation.
fields.correctAnswer: Idiom C does not actually filter rows — DataFrame.filter() selects COLUMNS (here just daily_kw via items=[...]); the row predicate is done by the .loc[...] that follows. Same row count by coincidence, very different operation.
fields.rationale: DataFrame.filter() is named misleadingly. It does not filter rows by predicate — it selects columns (or rows by index LABEL). The items=['daily_kw'] argument keeps only the daily_kw column. The actual row predicate in idiom C is the .loc[df['daily_kw'] > 1000] that follows. The 6-row match on this dataset is coincidental — change the test data and idiom C drops most of the columns the team expected to keep. The most common Junior confusion is reading 'filter' and assuming row predicate; in Pandas, filter() is a column-selection method.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Treats all three as the same operation. query() has its own parser; filter() does something entirely different — they are not aliases.

Option B: Identifies a real query() quirk but it is not what makes idiom C different on this dataset.

Option C: Mixes a real view-vs-copy concern with wrong attribution; the load-bearing fact is that filter() is not row-filtering at all.

tasks.crossReference: Foundations curriculum: Filtering chapter, 'Method names that lie' section. Tool-specific extensions: Pandas Junior Recognition Track PJR1.4 (same idioms with deeper view-vs-copy analysis); PySpark Junior Recognition Track has no equivalent because PySpark's filter() does what its name suggests.

tasks.title: Where Do The Nulls Go When You Sort?

description.context: When Pandas sorts a column that contains nulls, it has to decide where the nulls go. The default is na_position='last' — nulls always go to the END of the result, regardless of whether the sort is ascending or descending. Sort_values does NOT drop nulls; every input row appears in the output. This default differs from SQL conventions: many SQL dialects place nulls FIRST when sorting ascending and LAST when sorting descending. In Pandas the position is fixed (last) and direction-independent unless you pass na_position='first' explicitly.
description.task: What are the first three rows printed, in order?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 8-row sample of NordGrid meter readings. Three rows have null `daily_kw` (M-003, M-004, M-006).

fields.label: What are the first three rows printed, in order?
options: M-002, M-007, M-001 — sort_values silently drops nulls before sorting, so head(3) shows the three smallest non-null daily_kw values from a row-reduced 5-row frame.
M-002, M-007, M-001 — sort_values keeps all 8 rows and places nulls last (na_position='last' default), so head(3) returns the three smallest non-null values: 720.1, 880.3, 1250.5.
M-003, M-004, M-006 — Pandas places nulls FIRST when sorting ascending (NULLS FIRST default, like in PostgreSQL), so head(3) returns the three null rows.
M-003, M-004, M-006 — Pandas raises a warning when sorting a column with nulls and falls back to placing nulls first, with the warning suppressed in notebook output.
fields.correctAnswer: M-002, M-007, M-001 — sort_values keeps all 8 rows and places nulls last (na_position='last' default), so head(3) returns the three smallest non-null values: 720.1, 880.3, 1250.5.
fields.rationale: Pandas sort_values() places nulls at the END of the result by default (na_position='last'), regardless of sort direction, and does not drop them. So the first three rows are the smallest non-null values: M-002 (720.1), M-007 (880.3), M-001 (1250.5). The most common Junior confusion is importing the SQL mental model — many SQL dialects place NULLS FIRST when sorting ascending, but Pandas is null-last in BOTH directions unless you pass na_position='first'.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Believes sort_values silently drops nulls. It does not — dropping requires an explicit dropna().

Option C: Imports a SQL NULLS FIRST convention into Pandas. Pandas defaults to nulls-last regardless of direction.

Option D: Invents a warn-and-fallback behavior. Pandas sorts predictably with na_position='last' and never warns about null presence.

tasks.crossReference: Foundations curriculum: Sorting chapter, 'Null placement is a separate decision' section. Tool-specific extensions: SQL Junior Recognition Track SJR3.1 (NULLS FIRST vs NULLS LAST across PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Snowflake); PySpark Junior Recognition Track has the same default but with `asc_nulls_last()` / `asc_nulls_first()` as the explicit forms.

tasks.title: The Stable Sort That Was Not

description.context: A sort algorithm is STABLE if rows that compare equal on the sort key keep their original relative order. A classic trick to achieve 'group by A, ordered by B within each group' is to sort by B first, then sort by A — but this only works if the SECOND sort is stable. If the second sort is unstable, rows tied on A can be reordered arbitrarily, which destroys the B-ordering established by the first sort. Pandas sort_values supports several algorithms via the kind parameter: 'mergesort' and 'stable' are stable; 'quicksort' (the default) is NOT stable; 'heapsort' is also not stable.
description.task: Where is the bug, and why does it produce out-of-order rows within regions?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 8-row sample of NordGrid meter readings used to illustrate the bug.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Two-step sort intended to produce: grouped by region, ordered by daily_kw within each region.
step1 = df.sort_values(by='daily_kw', ascending=True)
result = step1.sort_values(by='region', ascending=True, kind='quicksort')

# Spec: within each region, daily_kw must be ascending.
# Observation: some regions have daily_kw out of order in the result.

fields.label: Where is the bug, and why does it produce out-of-order rows within regions?
options: The bug is kind='quicksort' on the second sort — quicksort is not stable, so rows tied on region can be reordered arbitrarily and the daily_kw ordering from step1 is destroyed. Use kind='mergesort' (or kind='stable') instead.
The bug is the order of the two sort calls — sorting by daily_kw first then by region overwrites the daily_kw ordering. The two sort_values calls should be swapped (region first, daily_kw second).

The bug is ascending=True on both sorts — when two consecutive sort_values calls share a direction, Pandas internally fuses them in reverse order and the second column's ordering wins, dropping the first.
There is no bug — sort_values output is intentionally non-deterministic when applied twice. The fix is to use a single sort_values(by=['region','daily_kw']) call instead of chaining.
fields.correctAnswer: The bug is kind='quicksort' on the second sort — quicksort is not stable, so rows tied on region can be reordered arbitrarily and the daily_kw ordering from step1 is destroyed. Use kind='mergesort' (or kind='stable') instead.
fields.rationale: The pattern 'sort by secondary key, then sort by primary key' produces grouped-and-ordered output IF AND ONLY IF the second sort is stable — meaning rows tied on the primary key retain their order from the previous sort. Quicksort is not stable, so step2 can reorder rows within each region group, destroying step1's daily_kw ordering. Switching to kind='mergesort' or kind='stable' fixes it. The most common Junior confusion is assuming all sort algorithms preserve previous orderings on ties — only stable ones do.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Swapping the calls would break it further — the secondary-then-primary pattern is the textbook way and it depends on the second sort being stable, not on call order.

Option C: Invents a fused-reverse-order rule that does not exist. Each sort_values call is independent.

Option D: Claims sort_values is non-deterministic. It is deterministic given a stable kind; the 'no bug' framing is the trap for students who never learned about stability.

tasks.title: Pivot With Duplicate Keys

description.context: Pandas has two reshape methods that look similar but behave differently when keys repeat. pivot() requires the (index, columns) pair to be UNIQUE — if any two rows share the same combination it has no rule to pick a single cell value, so it raises ValueError. pivot_table() is the aggregating cousin: it accepts duplicate keys and applies an aggfunc (default 'mean') to combine them. So pivot is for already-unique long data, pivot_table is for data that needs aggregation as part of the reshape. The error pivot raises is the engine refusing to silently choose between conflicting values.
description.task: What happens when this pivot() call runs against the 5-row dataset?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 5-row sample with a duplicate (meter_id, date) pair: M-002 has two readings on 2026-03-01.

fields.label: What happens when this pivot() call runs against the 5-row dataset?
options: Returns a wide DataFrame; M-002's 2026-03-01 cell holds 3210.0 — pivot() resolves duplicates by last-write-wins (SQL UPDATE-style), silently overwriting the first reading.
Returns a wide DataFrame; M-002's 2026-03-01 cell holds 6410.0 — pivot() sums duplicate (index, columns) pairs by default to preserve total energy across re-reads.

Raises ValueError ('Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape') — pivot() requires (index, columns) to be unique and refuses to silently choose between the two M-002/2026-03-01 values. Use pivot_table() if aggregation is intended.
Returns a wide DataFrame; M-002's 2026-03-01 cell holds the Python list [3200.0, 3210.0] — pivot() collects duplicates into an array so no value is lost.
fields.correctAnswer: Raises ValueError ('Index contains duplicate entries, cannot reshape') — pivot() requires (index, columns) to be unique and refuses to silently choose between the two M-002/2026-03-01 values. Use pivot_table() if aggregation is intended.
fields.rationale: pivot() raises ValueError when the (index, columns) pair is not unique. It refuses to silently pick a winner because there is no single correct answer in the data. The fix is either to deduplicate beforehand or to call pivot_table(..., aggfunc=...) which combines duplicates explicitly. The most common Junior confusion is assuming pivot picks last-write-wins (a SQL UPDATE-style mental model) or silently sums (confusing pivot with pivot_table) — Pandas chose the safest behavior, which is to fail loud.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Imports a SQL UPDATE last-write-wins rule. Pandas pivot has no such rule — it refuses to choose.

Option B: Confuses pivot with pivot_table; pivot_table's default aggfunc is 'mean' not 'sum' anyway, so the value would be 3205.0.

Option D: Invents a list-collection behavior. No mainstream pivot operation changes the cell type to a list.

tasks.crossReference: Foundations curriculum: Reshaping chapter, 'Pivot is not idempotent on duplicates' section. Tool-specific extensions: SQL Junior Recognition Track SJR4.2 (PIVOT in SQL Server / DuckDB, where the aggregation function is mandatory by syntax — a different way to force the same decision); PySpark Junior Recognition Track PJSR5.1 (pivot in PySpark, where the same uniqueness assumption applies but the error surface differs).

tasks.title: Three Ways To Go Wide-To-Long

description.context: Wide-to-long reshape (also called 'unpivot' or 'melt') turns N value-columns into a single value-column with N times more rows. Different tools have different defaults for what to do with NULL cells in the source. Pandas melt() KEEPS them: every (id, value_var) pair produces an output row even if the value is null. Pandas stack() DROPS them by default — its dropna parameter defaults to True, so null cells are silently removed. SQL UNPIVOT is engine-dependent: DuckDB keeps nulls; some other dialects (older T-SQL) drop them by default and require INCLUDE NULLS to retain them. So 'unpivot' is not a single behavior — three idioms can produce three different row counts.
description.task: How do the three idioms differ in their handling of the null cells (M-002.Tue and M-003.Mon)?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 3-row wide-format sample. M-001 has all three days, M-002 has Tuesday null, M-003 has Monday null.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Three idioms targeting the same wide-to-long reshape.

# Idiom A — Pandas melt()
result_a = df.melt(id_vars=['meter_id'], value_vars=['Mon','Tue','Wed'],
                   var_name='date', value_name='daily_kw')

# Idiom B — Pandas stack() with reset_index
result_b = df.set_index('meter_id')[['Mon','Tue','Wed']].stack().reset_index()
result_b.columns = ['meter_id', 'date', 'daily_kw']

# Idiom C — SQL UNPIVOT (DuckDB syntax, run on the same data via a SQL engine)
# UNPIVOT df ON Mon, Tue, Wed INTO NAME date VALUE daily_kw

fields.label: How do the three idioms differ in their handling of the null cells (M-002.Tue and M-003.Mon)?
options: All three keep the null rows — reshape operations universally preserve every input cell, so all three idioms produce 9 rows (3 meters x 3 days) with two of those rows holding null daily_kw values.
All three drop the null rows — reshape operations universally treat nulls as 'no observation' and exclude them, so all three idioms produce 7 rows on this dataset.

Idiom A (melt) keeps nulls (9 rows), idiom B (stack) drops them silently because stack's dropna parameter defaults to True (7 rows), and idiom C is engine-dependent — DuckDB UNPIVOT keeps nulls; some SQL dialects drop them by default.
Idiom B (stack) keeps nulls, idiom A (melt) drops them silently, and idiom C raises an error — Pandas melt filters nulls and SQL UNPIVOT requires a non-null source by spec.
fields.correctAnswer: Idiom A (melt) keeps nulls (9 rows), idiom B (stack) drops them silently because stack's dropna parameter defaults to True (7 rows), and idiom C is engine-dependent — DuckDB UNPIVOT keeps nulls; some SQL dialects drop them by default.
fields.rationale: melt() preserves null cells — every (id, value_var) combination produces an output row regardless of value. Idiom A gives 9 rows (3 meters x 3 days) with two nulls. stack() defaults to dropna=True, so it silently drops the two null cells; idiom B gives 7 rows. SQL UNPIVOT differs by engine: DuckDB and modern T-SQL keep nulls; older dialects drop them and require INCLUDE NULLS. The most common Junior confusion is assuming 'unpivot' is a single behavior across tools — null-handling defaults are NOT interchangeable.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Believes all reshape ops preserve all input cells. stack() drops nulls by default — the universal-preservation rule is wrong.

Option B: Believes all reshape ops drop nulls. melt() does not drop them — applying a half-rule everywhere.

Option D: Reverses melt vs stack. Remembers 'one of them drops nulls' but assigns it to the wrong method.

tasks.title: Cast '12.5' To Int — What Happens?

description.context: Casting a string-typed column to integer is one of the most common cleanup steps, and three popular engines disagree on what to do when the input string contains a fractional part like '12.5'. Pandas .astype(int) is STRICT — it routes through Python's int() built-in, which rejects '12.5' with a ValueError because int() refuses to silently truncate. DuckDB's CAST(... AS INT) is LENIENT — it truncates toward zero and returns 12. PySpark's .cast('int') is SAFE-NULL — it returns null for any value it cannot parse cleanly, keeping the pipeline running but losing the value. Three engines, three recovery strategies for the same input.
description.task: What does each idiom produce for the value '12.5'?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 3-row sample showing a string column daily_kw_str that includes the value '12.5'.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Three idioms for casting daily_kw_str to integer.

# Idiom A — Pandas .astype(int)
result_a = df['daily_kw_str'].astype(int)

# Idiom B — SQL CAST AS INT (DuckDB on the same data)
# SELECT CAST(daily_kw_str AS INT) FROM df

# Idiom C — PySpark .cast('int')
from pyspark.sql.functions import col
result_c = spark_df.withColumn('daily_kw_int', col('daily_kw_str').cast('int'))

fields.label: What does each idiom produce for the value '12.5'?
options: All three engines produce 12 — every standard integer cast truncates the fractional part toward zero. Pandas, DuckDB, and PySpark are interchangeable here; the cast is universal and consistent.
All three engines produce 13 — banker's rounding (IEEE 754) applies during integer casts: .5 rounds to the nearest even integer, and 13 is the result for all three engines.

Pandas .astype(int) raises ValueError ('invalid literal for int() with base 10'), DuckDB CAST returns 12 (truncates toward zero), PySpark .cast('int') silently returns null. Three engines, three recovery strategies.
Pandas .astype(int) returns 12 by truncating, DuckDB CAST raises a conversion error refusing the value, and PySpark .cast('int') returns 13 by rounding.
fields.correctAnswer: Pandas .astype(int) raises ValueError ('invalid literal for int() with base 10'), DuckDB CAST returns 12 (truncates toward zero), PySpark .cast('int') silently returns null. Three engines, three recovery strategies.
fields.rationale: The three engines disagree on '12.5'. Pandas .astype(int) routes through Python's int() built-in which refuses to silently lose precision and raises ValueError. DuckDB CAST AS INT truncates toward zero, returning 12. PySpark .cast('int') is the safe-null variant — it returns null on parse failure to keep streaming pipelines running, but the bad value vanishes without a warning. The most common Junior confusion is assuming 'cast to int' is a single universal operation; in reality each engine picked a different point on the strict-vs-lenient spectrum.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Believes all int casts truncate. Pandas does not — it raises rather than silently truncate.

Option B: Applies floating-point banker's rounding to int casts. Int casts truncate or fail; they do not round.

Option D: Names the right engines but assigns the wrong behaviors — easy mistake when each engine documents this differently.

tasks.title: The Date That Was A String All Along

description.context: A column whose name contains the word 'date' is not necessarily of dtype datetime — it can still be plain string (object dtype). When you compare a string column against a string literal in Pandas, the comparison is LEXICOGRAPHIC: Pandas walks the two strings character by character and compares Unicode code points, stopping at the first difference. This works correctly for date comparison ONLY if every value is the same fixed-width ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD with zero-padded month and day). The moment a value has unpadded digits ('2026-01-9' instead of '2026-01-09'), the position of the digits no longer matches across rows and the lexicographic comparison gives wrong answers — even though the strings 'look like dates'.
description.task: Why does M-002 with date '2026-01-9' pass a filter for `>= '2026-01-10'`?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 5-row sample. Note the `date` column is stored as STRING despite its name, with mixed formatting: most values are zero-padded ('2026-01-15'), but one row (M-002) has unpadded day ('2026-01-9') from a different upstream source.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# The filter intent: keep meter readings dated on or after 2026-01-10.
result = df[df['date'] >= '2026-01-10']

# Result row count: 5 (all rows pass — including M-002 from January 9)
# Specification: keep ONLY rows from January 10 onward.

fields.label: Why does M-002 with date '2026-01-9' pass a filter for `>= '2026-01-10'`?
options: The date column holds strings; comparison is lexicographic. At position 8, '2026-01-9' has '9' and '2026-01-10' has '1' — '9' has a higher Unicode code point than '1', so the row passes >= '2026-01-10'. Fix: pd.to_datetime first.

Pandas applies date semantics regardless of column dtype, but the locale parses the threshold '2026-01-10' as YYYY-DD-MM (so it becomes October 1, 2026) and the row passes because every January date is before October.

Pandas auto-coerces both sides to datetime when a string column is compared to a string literal, but the coercion silently fails on the unpadded '2026-01-9' and the row is treated as null and retained by the >= operator.

The >= operator on string columns uses an internal numeric encoding that maps each character to its Unicode position; the resulting integer comparison is mathematically equivalent to the date comparison the teammate intended.
fields.correctAnswer: The date column holds strings; comparison is lexicographic. At position 8, '2026-01-9' has '9' and '2026-01-10' has '1' — '9' has a higher Unicode code point than '1', so the row passes >= '2026-01-10'. Fix: pd.to_datetime first.
fields.rationale: The values in the date column are strings (object dtype) despite the column name. df['date'] >= '2026-01-10' is a lexicographic string comparison, not a date comparison. The first 8 characters '2026-01-' match; at position 8 the row has '9' (Unicode 57) while the threshold has '1' (Unicode 49), so the row compares as greater. Lexicographic comparison only matches date semantics when every value is fixed-width zero-padded ISO. The most common Junior confusion is assuming a column named 'date' has datetime semantics — only the dtype determines that, not the name. Always cast with pd.to_datetime before comparing.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents a locale-driven date-parsing on string-vs-string comparisons. Pandas does no such parsing here.

Option C: Believes Pandas auto-coerces strings to dates and treats parse failures as null. It does neither — string-on-string stays string-on-string.

Option D: Claims lexicographic comparison equals date comparison. Only true on fixed-width zero-padded ISO; breaks on '2026-01-9'.

tasks.title: Cleaning Operations Have Order Dependencies

description.context: Pandas dropna() takes a `subset` parameter and a `how` parameter, and they interact in a way Junior engineers often misread. By default `how='any'` — meaning a row is dropped if ANY column in the subset is null. So passing subset=['meter_id', 'region'] does NOT mean 'drop rows missing meter_id, then handle region separately'; it means 'drop rows where meter_id OR region is null'. The opposite mode `how='all'` only drops rows where every subset column is null. To drop on a single column the subset must contain ONLY that column. This bug is invisible at runtime because no error is raised — the only symptom is fewer rows than expected reaching the next step.
description.task: Why does the result contain fewer 'UNKNOWN' regions than QA expected?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.caption: 6-row Bronze sample. M-002 has missing meter_id (unrecoverable). M-003 and M-005 have missing region (recoverable — should become 'UNKNOWN'). M-006 has both missing (unrecoverable due to meter_id).

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
# Spec: drop rows where meter_id is missing, then fill missing region with 'UNKNOWN'.
step1 = df.dropna(subset=['meter_id', 'region'])
step2 = step1.fillna({'region': 'UNKNOWN'})
result = step2

fields.label: Why does the result contain fewer 'UNKNOWN' regions than QA expected?
options: fillna uses the wrong syntax — Pandas expects fillna(value='UNKNOWN', subset=['region']) not the dict form, so fillna runs on every column and the 'UNKNOWN' count gets diluted.

The dropna subset is too wide — with default how='any', subset=['meter_id','region'] drops a row if EITHER column is null, so the rows with only region missing are dropped here too and never reach fillna. Fix: subset=['meter_id'] only.

fillna's value 'UNKNOWN' is a Python string but region was silently cast to categorical earlier, so fillna fails on type mismatch and the missing-region rows end up as the string 'nan' instead of 'UNKNOWN'.
The pipeline assigns result = step2 but should assign result = df — a name-shadowing bug where step2 is computed correctly but the wrong variable reaches result, leaving original nulls intact.
fields.correctAnswer: The dropna subset is too wide — with default how='any', subset=['meter_id','region'] drops a row if EITHER column is null, so the rows with only region missing are dropped here too and never reach fillna. Fix: subset=['meter_id'] only.
fields.rationale: dropna defaults to how='any', meaning 'drop if ANY column in the subset is null'. Passing subset=['meter_id', 'region'] therefore drops both unrecoverable rows (missing meter_id) AND the recoverable ones (only region missing) — the latter group never reaches fillna. The fix is dropna(subset=['meter_id']) so only meter_id-missing rows are dropped, leaving region-missing rows for the fillna step. The most common Junior confusion is reading 'subset=[A, B]' as 'apply this stage to A separately, then to B' — but it is one combined predicate, OR'd by default.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents a wrong fillna signature. The dict form fillna({'region': 'UNKNOWN'}) is valid and common.

Option C: Fabricates a categorical cast not present in the snippet. region is a regular string column.

Option D: The assignment chain step1=..., step2=..., result=step2 is correct and free of shadowing — picking D is grasping at a generic suspicion.

tasks.title: The 30-Line Bronze-To-Silver Cleaning Pipeline

description.context: Cleaning pipelines mix two kinds of operations: VALUE changes (the cell contents are different after) and DTYPE changes (the column's storage type is different after). pd.to_datetime parses an ISO string into a datetime64 representation — same instant in time, different storage type. That is a pure dtype change. By contrast pd.to_numeric(..., errors='coerce') changes BOTH dtype (object to float64) AND values (anything unparseable becomes NaN). String methods like str.upper() and str.strip() change values but leave dtype untouched (object stays object). Telling the two apart is a key reading-comprehension skill for cleaning code reviews.
description.task: Which line is the only line that changes the dtype of a column rather than its values?

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
import pandas as pd
from pandas.api.types import is_numeric_dtype

# Line 1: read raw Bronze CSV (intentionally permissive — accepts mixed empty/null)
df = pd.read_csv('bronze/meters_2026-03-02.csv', keep_default_na=False, na_values=[''])

# Line 2: drop rows that are unrecoverable (no meter_id)
df = df.dropna(subset=['meter_id'])

# Line 3: standardize region casing — vendors send mixed case
df['region'] = df['region'].str.upper()

# Line 4: trim whitespace from string columns
for col in ['meter_id', 'region', 'customer_type', 'substation_id']:
    df[col] = df[col].str.strip()

# Line 5: parse the date column from string to datetime
df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['date'], format='%Y-%m-%d')

# Line 6: cast daily_kw to float, coercing parse failures to null
df['daily_kw'] = pd.to_numeric(df['daily_kw'], errors='coerce')

# Line 7: deduplicate exact duplicates (same meter, same date, same value)
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['meter_id', 'date', 'daily_kw'])

# Line 8: fill missing region with the literal 'UNKNOWN' (recoverable downstream)
df['region'] = df['region'].fillna('UNKNOWN')

# Line 9: keep only the columns Silver needs
df = df[['meter_id', 'daily_kw', 'date', 'region', 'customer_type', 'substation_id']]

# Line 10: write Silver in Parquet with snappy compression
df.to_parquet('silver/meters_2026-03-02.parquet', compression='snappy', index=False)

fields.label: Which line is the only line that changes the dtype of a column rather than its values?
options: Line 3 (str.upper()) — uppercasing produces a new string array that Pandas tags with a refreshed dtype, so this is a dtype-only change even though the textual content is reinterpreted.
Line 6 (pd.to_numeric(errors='coerce')) — the cast from string to numeric is the only true dtype change; the other lines stay within object dtype and only modify values.
Line 4 (str.strip()) — whitespace trimming is the canonical Pandas dtype refresh on string columns; values stay the same, only the dtype is reset.

Line 5 (pd.to_datetime) — this is the only line whose primary effect is dtype (object to datetime64) without changing the underlying instants. Line 6 changes dtype too but ALSO changes values via errors='coerce'.
fields.correctAnswer: Line 5 (pd.to_datetime) — this is the only line whose primary effect is dtype (object to datetime64) without changing the underlying instants. Line 6 changes dtype too but ALSO changes values via errors='coerce'.
fields.rationale: Line 5 is the cleanest dtype-only change. The string '2026-03-01' and the datetime64 representation of March 1, 2026 are the SAME instant — only the storage type changes. Line 6 (pd.to_numeric with errors='coerce') does change dtype but it ALSO changes values: any unparseable string becomes NaN. The most common Junior confusion is treating 'cast' lines as a single category — but coerce-on-error makes line 6 a hybrid (type change + value change), while line 5 is pure type change.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Believes str.upper() refreshes dtype. It does not — output stays object dtype.

Option B: Half-right — line 6 IS a dtype change, but the question asks for the ONLY-dtype line; line 6 also mutates values via coerce.

Option C: Invents a 'dtype refresh on strip'. str.strip changes values; dtype is unchanged.
